stem: A client with diabetes and hypertension says, 'My kidneys must be fine because I don't have any urinary symptoms.' Which response by the nurse is best?

options.A: Kidney screening can wait until swelling or urine changes develop.
options.B: A normal urine appearance rules out early chronic kidney disease.
options.C: Only a serum creatinine level is needed to screen for chronic kidney disease.
options.D: Early kidney disease may have no symptoms, so at-risk clients are screened with kidney-function and urine-albumin testing.

rationale: NIDDK identifies diabetes and hypertension as major CKD risk factors and notes that early kidney disease may have no symptoms; testing may be the only way to detect it. NIDDK recommends screening people at risk using urine albumin assessment and estimated GFR from serum creatinine. Therefore D is correct. A delays detection until symptomatic disease, B incorrectly relies on urine appearance, and C omits urine albumin, one of the two key CKD markers.
educational_objective: Teach clients with CKD risk factors that early disease can be asymptomatic and that screening includes assessment of both eGFR and urine albumin.
source_organization: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), NIH
source_document_title: Identify & Evaluate Patients with Chronic Kidney Disease; Preventing Chronic Kidney Disease
source_locator: Identify & Evaluate Patients with CKD > Identify Patients with CKD: screen people at risk including diabetes and hypertension; two key markers are urine albumin and eGFR. Preventing CKD: early kidney disease may have no symptoms, so getting tested may be the only way to know kidney health; manage conditions such as diabetes and high blood pressure.
source_claim_supported: Diabetes and hypertension increase CKD risk; early CKD may be asymptomatic, and at-risk screening uses both urine albumin and eGFR assessment.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance: provide education and care for prevention and early detection of health problems; identify risk factors and recommended screening based on client needs.
blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — CKD risk recognition and early screening
correction_summary: Replaced generic prevention advice with a realistic asymptomatic at-risk client teaching scenario grounded in NIDDK's risk-factor and screening guidance.
audit_findings: NIDDK directly supports risk factors, asymptomatic early disease, and combined urine-albumin/eGFR screening. D uniquely answers the misconception; A-C each omit or contradict a key screening principle. No universal screening interval or target is asserted. Blueprint is an appropriate Health Promotion and Maintenance fit. Independent adversarial second pass found no second answer, cueing, ambiguity or unsupported precision.
